title: Bamboo Paper Stamp Mill
note: SUT-facing prompt stream. Read segments in order; no labels are provided by design.

segments.prompt: At dusk, Bailu（A forty-year-old papermaking master, blue-cloth headwrap, hemp apron soaked in pulp, hands blanched from soaking, wrists steady and precise） rolls up the bamboo curtain door, enters the damp papermaking workshop（A bright papermaking workshop, rows of bamboo-pulp vats, mold frames and screen beds along the walls, air thick with bamboo and lime smell）, and lays the bamboo papermaking screen（A fine bamboo papermaking screen, wires even and straight, old bamboo frame polished bright, surface coated with even white pulp） flat on the screen bed.

Five rows of wooden paper-drying clamp rods（Five rows of wooden paper-drying clamp rods hung neatly under the workshop beams, used to clamp freshly lifted wet sheets） hang under the workshop beams; Bailu checks each row to see if the clamps will hold wet paper.

By the waterwheel two waterwheel wooden hammers（Two wooden hammers linked to the waterwheel that fall in turn as the wheel turns, pounding cooked bamboo in the stone trough） fall in turn; Bailu listens to their rhythm pounding cooked bamboo.
Bailu dips the papermaking screen into the bamboo-pulp vat and gives a gentle shake, spreading a thin white pulp across the screen.
He lifts the first wet sheet onto the wall board, leaving tiny water beads on his fingertips.
Bailu unties the bamboo-sheath cord and opens the oil-paper-covered pulp formula book（An oil-paper-covered pulp formula book recording bamboo soak days, steaming hours, and lime ratios）.
With pine-soot ink he records today's bamboo soak days, lime ratio, and paper batch number.
Bailu closes the formula book and leans the damp bamboo papermaking screen by the vat to drain.

At the bamboo-soaking pond（A bamboo-soaking pond outside the village, green bamboo tubes floating on the water, lime, bamboo strips, and freshly peeled bamboo sheaths stacked at the bank） in the morning, Bailu greets young apprentice Mili（A fifteen-year-old apprentice girl in a plant-dyed apron, bamboo-strip bracelet on her wrist, fingertips often marked with white pulp） pushing the green-bamboo pulp cart（A long narrow green-bamboo pulp cart, wooden trough holding softened bamboo fiber, sides lined with green bamboo-leaf sheaths, four small wooden wheels below）.
Mili steadies the pulp cart; softened bamboo fiber in the wooden trough rocks gently with the water.

Bailu leans three watermark sieve（Three fine bamboo watermark sieves with shallow patterns set into the mesh, leaning by the vat in the papermaking workshop）s against the stone steps by the pond and teaches Mili to check whether the sieve patterns have broken lines.
Mili lifts the green bamboo-leaf sheaths along the pulp cart and checks whether wet bamboo fiber has tangled the wheels.

In the paper-drying gallery（The mill's paper-drying gallery, wooden racks on both sides hung with half-dry white sheets, heat, paper scent, and vapor mingled together）, Aye（A youth whose face closely resembles Mili's, but wearing charcoal-black sleeve covers and a deep-brown apron, expression bold） in charcoal-black sleeve covers looks back from behind half-dry white sheets.
Aye flicks his deep-brown apron with a fingertip, deliberately showing the black ash on his sleeve covers.
He pulls out a bamboo clamp; the white paper trembles lightly in the heat.
Vapor at the gallery's end hides Aye's face; only the deep-brown apron moves among the paper shadows.
By the bamboo-soaking pond, Mili and Aye move bamboo tubes together—one in a plant-dyed apron, one in charcoal-black sleeve covers.
Mili guards the bamboo-strip bracelet on her wrist; Aye ties his deep-brown apron tighter.
They face each other across the pond a moment, then carry bamboo tubes to different vats.
On a mountain-rain night months later, Bailu alone watches the vat in the papermaking workshop, the bamboo papermaking screen against his knee.

He opens the pulp formula book（The same pulp formula book soaked through by wet pulp, oil-paper cover wrinkled, ink characters blurred into gray-white blobs） and finds wet pulp has crept from the desk corner; the oil-paper cover wrinkles, ink characters blur into gray-white blobs.
Bailu scrapes pulp stains from the page edges with a bamboo slip and rewrites the still-readable ratios from memory.
Through the long papermaking season, Bailu day after day dips screens, lifts sheets, and presses out water in the workshop.
When plum rains arrive, he moves the paper-drying clamp rods farther apart so wet sheets will not re-dampen and wrinkle.
As new bamboo comes to market, Bailu stands in the doorway watching bundles of green bamboo carried to the pond.
At high summer noon he fans heat from freshly lifted sheets with a cattail fan.
In endless autumn rain, lime smell and green-bamboo scent hang by the pulp vat.
On another New Year's Eve, Bailu alone keeps watch in the workshop until the waterwheel falls silent.
At dawn Bailu patrols along the bamboo-soaking pond; the green-bamboo pulp cart rests by the stone steps.
He crouches to check the pulp cart's four small wooden wheels, confirming none are jammed by bamboo fiber.
Bailu restacks scattered bamboo-strip bundles by the pond, leaving a path for the cart.

A cedar drying cart（A cedar drying cart clamping half-dry paper sheets, with no green bamboo-leaf sheaths and holding no bamboo fiber） rolls in from the gallery direction, clamping half-dry paper sheets, but with no green bamboo-leaf sheaths and holding no bamboo fiber.
A mountain flood suddenly overruns the pond's stone steps; bamboo tubes and sheaths are swept up in muddy water.

Bailu snatches the bamboo papermaking screen（The same bamboo papermaking screen with several wires snapped, frame cracked by floodwater, dried pulp crust jammed in the seams） from the workshop doorway, only to see the frame cracked by the current and the screen wires snapped.
The green-bamboo pulp cart is shoved off the stone steps by the flood; bamboo fiber in the trough surges and spills.

The green-bamboo pulp cart（The green-bamboo pulp cart smashed by floodwater, trough split, bamboo-leaf sheaths scattered, only one small wooden wheel jammed beside the stone steps） smashes into the waterwheel base and breaks into slats; bamboo-leaf sheaths and one small wooden wheel drift into the muddy water.
Bailu clutches the torn papermaking screen and retreats into the workshop, wet pulp dripping down his apron.
The day after the flood, Bailu stands in the workshop staring at the screen-torn bamboo papermaking screen.
On a blank page of the pulp formula book he records the moment the green-bamboo pulp cart wrecked and was scrapped, ink pressed over pulp stains.
A bundle of green bamboo-leaf sheaths fallen from the green-bamboo pulp cart hangs by the wall; Bailu does not discard them for a long time.
Bailu takes one row from the five rows of paper-drying clamp rods under the beams and clamps a half-wet paper sample salvaged from the flood.
He places the remaining small wooden wheel from the green-bamboo pulp cart into a wooden box and covers it with old cloth.
Weeks later Bailu brings in an old bamboo craftsman to remeasure screen wires beside the workshop vat.

The craftsman first offers a coarse screen mold frame（A coarse bamboo mold frame shaped like a papermaking screen, but with sparse wires and no worn polish on the old bamboo frame） for comparison—similar in shape, but sparse wires and no worn polish on the old bamboo frame.

Fine bamboo wires are worked into the tears one by one; the bamboo papermaking screen（The bamboo papermaking screen restrung tight, missing wires replaced, old bamboo frame pinned with new bamboo nails, pulp surface smooth again） is restrung tight and the surface smooths again.
Bailu dips the repaired papermaking screen into the vat with a light shake and lifts a wet sheet with even edges.

A clay-jar handcart（A low cart pushing a clay jar of clear water and lime, holding no bamboo fiber—definitely not the green-bamboo pulp cart） rolls up to the pond; the jar holds only clear water and lime—it is not the already wrecked and scrapped green-bamboo pulp cart.

The paper-shop bookkeeper（A lean bookkeeper also in a blue-cloth headwrap, but with abacus beads pinned at the cuff, build close to Bailu's） steps beside Bailu to check paper batches; both wear blue-cloth headwraps, backs alike for a moment.
The bookkeeper points at the clay-jar handcart to arrange lime storage; Bailu keeps checking bamboo stock in the pond.

Suner（A bamboo-sheath peeler girl from the next village in a light-brown apron, at a glance like young Mili, but wearing a bamboo hairpin and shy-eyed） from the next village carries bamboo sheaths to the pond; her light-brown apron from afar looks like young Mili's plant-dyed apron.
Suner tries to push a bamboo tube into the water, but Bailu shakes his head, noting her bamboo hairpin—she is not Mili after all.

At dusk years later, Bailu（The same Bailu: forearm scalded by boiling pulp and wrapped in herbal cloth, leaning on a broken bamboo cane, one corner of the hemp apron charred） leans on a broken bamboo cane and slowly enters the half-collapsed abandoned water-powered stamp mill（A half-collapsed stamp mill, waterwheel stopped, wooden hammers hanging above the stone trough, moss thick in the corners）.
By the stopped waterwheel those two wooden hammers still hang above the stone trough, swaying lightly when the wind blows.
Bailu rests his herbal-cloth-wrapped forearm on the stone trough edge and hears distant water like the old pulp-pounding rhythm.

By day, adult Mili（A woman master in her early twenties, still in the plant-dyed apron and bamboo-strip bracelet, upright posture, able to lift a full wet sheet in one motion） returns to the village gate with a new screen bed on her back and hurries toward the abandoned water-powered stamp mill.
Under the stamp-mill door Mili reunites with cane-leaning Bailu; they embrace across the vapor.
By the wooden cot Mili holds Bailu's herbal-cloth-wrapped forearm and listens to rain beyond the waterwheel.

Bailu（Bailu lies still with eyes closed on a wooden cot in the water-powered stamp mill, the hemp apron covering his chest）'s breath grows weak; at last he closes his eyes and quietly dies of illness in the stamp mill.
Behind the papermaking workshop door Bailu's old hemp apron still hangs; Mili strokes the charred corner.

Mili stands before the Bai-ji wooden plaque（A wooden plaque hung over the workshop lintel, carved with 'Bai-ji Paper Mill', corners swollen by damp）; the year Bailu carved by hand has swollen open with damp.
She wipes clean the wooden plaque Bailu left and pins the swollen corners back to the lintel with bamboo nails.

Aye（Aye after remaking his look still wears charcoal-black sleeve covers, a steam-scald scar on his brow, deep-brown apron swapped for a leather-buckle cut） with his remade look walks up from outside the stamp mill; the steam-scald scar on his brow gleams in shadow.
Mili and Aye stand side by side before the old waterwheel—one bamboo-strip bracelet on a wrist, one charcoal-black sleeve cover on an arm.
The shot returns to years ago—that apprentice girl checking the green-bamboo-leaf cart wheels appears again.
The opening moment returns—in the workshop a bamboo screen dips into the white-pulp vat for the first time.
Flashback to the paper-drying gallery—that similar figure in charcoal-black sleeve covers slips past behind the white sheets.
Again those five rows of wooden rods clamping wet paper under the workshop beams appear.
Back to that shallow bamboo-soaking pond of first meeting, green bamboo tubes floating on the water as before.
Mili opens that pulp-smeared pulp formula book and writes a new paper batch number on a clean fresh page.
Five rows of paper-drying clamp rods still hang neat under the beams; freshly lifted wet sheets gleam between the clamps.
By the vat those three watermark sieves still lean in place, sieve patterns unbroken.
Mili grips the restrung-repaired bamboo papermaking screen and bends to lift a thin, even wet sheet.
